extracted.subtask_description: Designing and placing a single recurring visual joke (a 'runner') that appears three times in a ~22-minute sitcom episode, escalating to a payoff. Guidance covers anatomy, rules, design steps, anti-patterns, and cross-episode considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Runner joke (definition)
rubrics_metrics.description: One small beat that appears 3 times in an episode, escalating each time in absurdity or payoff. Distinct from series callbacks (span episodes) and one-off gags (appear once).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every great sitcom episode has a runner — a single recurring element that appears three times over the episode's 22 minutes, escalating in absurdity or payoff each time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three beats (setup → return → payoff)
rubrics_metrics.description: A runner has three beats: Beat 1 — Setup (planted early); Beat 2 — Return (reappears mid-episode, slightly escalated); Beat 3 — Payoff (final appearance, maximum absurdity or reversal). All three beats must be recognizably the same element/frame but escalate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing: Beat 1 in Act 1, Beat 2 around mid-Act 2, Beat 3 in Act 3 or the tag. The audience experiences a drumbeat: setup → return → payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tightly visual
rubrics_metrics.description: A runner must have a strong visual signature so the audience recognizes it instantly; it should be an image/action, not an abstract concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not a concept, an image. The runner should be instantly visible and identifiable without requiring conceptual explanation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Short beats: ≤ 5 seconds each
rubrics_metrics.description: Each appearance of the runner should be quick — under five seconds of screen time per beat.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep each beat < 5 seconds to preserve the rhythm; longer beats break the runner's drumbeat effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Escalation, not repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Each return must raise stakes or absurdity; if beat 3 is structurally identical to beat 1, it's repetition, not a runner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat 3 should escalate or reverse the pattern. If the third beat is the same as the first, it's a repeated joke and a sign of weak writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: One runner per episode
rubrics_metrics.description: Limit to exactly one runner in an episode to avoid competing patterns that dilute audience recognition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Two runners compete for pattern-recognition. Pick one runner and commit to it per episode.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routed through a specific character (externalizes the character's Lie)
rubrics_metrics.description: Runners should be associated with one character and externalize that character's 'Lie' (core trait or motivation) so the gag feels organic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Runners usually belong to one character. Example: a laser-pointer runner belongs to 老周 because it externalizes his 'I'm running this meeting' Lie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tag option (save payoff for tag)
rubrics_metrics.description: If the episode has a tag (post-credits beat), you may save the payoff for the tag to compress the runner's escalation into a tight final moment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using a tag: save the payoff for the tag. The audience re-experiences the runner's escalation in a compressed moment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: pick the character (engine of the runner)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose the character whose Lie is the strongest driver of the episode; that character should own the runner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which character has the strongest Lie in this episode? Their Lie is the runner's engine — start here.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: find the image (visual object/action)
rubrics_metrics.description: Select a concrete visual object or action (not a concept) that externalizes the chosen character's Lie.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not the concept ('control freak'), the image (a calculator). A visual object/action that externalizes their Lie.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: plot three beats as single lines
rubrics_metrics.description: Write beats as single-line descriptions: Beat 1 straightforward; Beat 2 in a slightly broken context; Beat 3 in a maximally broken context or reversed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beat 1: [character] does [action] — straightforward, world functional. Beat 2: [character] does [action] — slightly broken context. Beat 3: [character] does [action] — maximally broken context OR reversed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: space beats across acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Place Beat 1 in Act 1, Beat 2 mid-Act 2, Beat 3 in Act 3 or the tag to create proper episodic rhythm.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Step 4 — Space them through the episode: Beat 1 in Act 1, Beat 2 in Act 2 midpoint, Beat 3 in Act 3 or tag.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design: ensure no dialogue explanation needed
rubrics_metrics.description: The runner should operate visually and pattern-wise so the audience recognizes it without characters calling attention to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a character has to say 'haha, the laser again?' you've failed. The audience should get the joke from the pattern alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cross-episode runner criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Cross-episode runners (callbacks across multiple episodes) are rarer and riskier; follow constraints if attempted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plant subtly in early episodes; don't explicitly flag it until payoff episode; payoff must be strong enough to justify patience; don't overuse — one cross-episode runner per series max.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: punchline repetition
rubrics_metrics.description: Repeating the same punchline three times is not a runner but lazy repetition (meme-stuck writing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Same punchline three times isn't a runner; each beat must differ in context, stake, or reversal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: runner that needs explanation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the third beat requires a character to explain 'this is the third time,' the runner has failed to function for the audience.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Runner that needs explanation: if beat 3 requires characters to point out the pattern, it fails to operate on the audience's subconscious.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: runner lost in crowded B-plot
rubrics_metrics.description: Runners can be buried if the episode juggles too many plots simultaneously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If your episode has 3 plots running, the runner can get buried. Simplify plots or abandon the runner.

rubrics_metrics.name: Anti-pattern: runner that contradicts character
rubrics_metrics.description: A runner must be something the character would actually do; if it contradicts established character traits, it will feel false.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The runner must be something this character would actually do or carry. A laser pointer runner only works for 老周 because he's established as the management-performance guy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checklist (summary of must-haves)
rubrics_metrics.description: A concise checklist of requirements: Exactly one runner per episode; three beats, each < 5 seconds; Beat 3 escalates or reverses; runner visually recognizable without dialogue; routed through one specific character; beats spaced Act1/Act2/Act3-or-tag; runner externalizes the character's Lie; if using tag, payoff in the tag.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this checklist as a final validation before locking the draft.
